samples.refined_query: Show the names and countries of singers who performed in concerts in 2014.
samples.sql: SELECT DISTINCT s.Name, s.Country FROM singer s JOIN singer_in_concert sic ON s.Singer_ID = sic.Singer_ID JOIN concert c ON sic.concert_ID = c.concert_ID WHERE c.Year = 2014
expected_reasonings: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. All columns (Name, Country, Singer_ID, concert_ID, Year) exist in the APS schema. Both JOINs use valid ON clauses. DISTINCT is correctly applied because the bridge table singer_in_concert can produce duplicate singer rows. WHERE filters on concert.Year = 2014, which matches the user's intent. No forbidden constructs or MySQL-specific syntax detected.

[OK] Query is valid. The 3-table JOIN chain (singer -> singer_in_concert -> concert) is correct with proper ON clauses. DISTINCT prevents duplicate singer entries from the bridge table. Year=2014 filter matches the question. All referenced columns are in the APS schema. No PostgreSQL incompatibilities.

[OK] APPROVED. Schema compliance confirmed: Name, Country, Singer_ID, concert_ID, Year all present. JOIN structure is sound, DISTINCT is necessary due to the many-to-many bridge table, and WHERE Year=2014 aligns with the user's intent. Valid PostgreSQL 14+ syntax.

samples.sql: SELECT Song_Name FROM singer WHERE Age > (SELECT AVG(Age) FROM singer)
expected_reasonings: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. Song_Name and Age exist in the APS schema for singer. The scalar subquery computes AVG(Age) over the same table, directly matching the user's intent of 'above the average age'. No SELECT *, no DML, no forbidden constructs. AVG() and scalar subqueries are valid PostgreSQL syntax.

[OK] Valid query. Both Song_Name and Age are confirmed in the singer schema. The WHERE clause uses a scalar subquery SELECT AVG(Age) FROM singer to filter above-average singers. This correctly implements the user's intent. Valid PostgreSQL 14+ syntax with no violations.

samples.refined_query: Show the names of singers who have not performed in any concert.
samples.sql: SELECT Name FROM singer WHERE Singer_ID NOT IN (SELECT Singer_ID FROM singer_in_concert)
expected_reasonings: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. Name and Singer_ID exist in singer; Singer_ID exists in singer_in_concert. NOT IN with a scalar subquery correctly implements exclusion semantics — singers absent from singer_in_concert have not performed. This directly answers 'who have not performed in any concert'. Valid PostgreSQL syntax, no forbidden constructs.

[OK] Valid query. Name and Singer_ID are in the singer schema; Singer_ID is confirmed in singer_in_concert. The NOT IN subquery correctly identifies singers absent from the concert participation table. Semantics match the user's question. No violations.

[OK] APPROVED. The anti-join via NOT IN returns singers whose Singer_ID does not appear in singer_in_concert, meaning they have never performed. All columns exist in the APS schema. No SELECT *, no DML, no forbidden constructs. Valid PostgreSQL 14+.

samples.refined_query: Show stadium names and the highest year of concerts held in each stadium.
samples.sql: SELECT T2.name, MAX(T1.year) FROM concert AS T1 JOIN stadium AS T2 ON T1.stadium_id = T2.stadium_id GROUP BY T1.stadium_id, T2.name
expected_reasonings: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. year and stadium_id exist in concert; name and stadium_id exist in stadium. JOIN ON stadium_id is valid. MAX(year) correctly answers 'highest year'. GROUP BY stadium_id and name groups per venue. PostgreSQL requires all non-aggregated SELECT columns to appear in GROUP BY — T2.name is included. No forbidden constructs.

[OK] Valid query. Concert and stadium are joined on stadium_id. MAX(T1.year) returns the latest year per stadium. GROUP BY T1.stadium_id, T2.name satisfies PostgreSQL's strict requirement that all non-aggregated SELECT expressions appear in GROUP BY. All columns exist in the APS schema.

[OK] APPROVED. The JOIN is correct and MAX(year) answers the 'highest year' question. PostgreSQL 14+ requires T2.name in GROUP BY since it appears in SELECT without being aggregated — it is correctly included. Year, Stadium_ID (concert), Name, Stadium_ID (stadium) are all in the schema.

samples.refined_query: What percentage of singers are male?
samples.sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN Is_male = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FLOAT) * 100.0 / COUNT(Singer_ID) FROM singer
expected_reasonings: [OK] Validation: APPROVED. Is_male and Singer_ID exist in the APS schema. CAST AS FLOAT is valid PostgreSQL syntax for floating-point division. Is_male = TRUE is the correct PostgreSQL boolean comparison (not 1/0). CASE WHEN counts male singers and divides by total COUNT(Singer_ID) — this produces the percentage asked for. No forbidden constructs.

[OK] Valid query. Is_male and Singer_ID are confirmed in the singer schema. CAST AS FLOAT ensures decimal division in PostgreSQL. Is_male = TRUE is the correct boolean literal syntax (not MySQL-style is_male=1). COUNT(Singer_ID) gives the total and the CASE expression counts males. No violations.

[OK] APPROVED. The percentage calculation is correct for PostgreSQL: SUM(CASE WHEN Is_male=TRUE) counts males, CAST AS FLOAT prevents integer division, multiplied by 100.0 and divided by COUNT(Singer_ID) gives the percentage. Both Is_male and Singer_ID are in the APS schema. No forbidden constructs.
